newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia announces near-free trade status.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia announces near-free trade status.

text.p: Mongolia unveiled sweeping tax reforms on Monday to turn the nation on the steppes of Central Asia into a virtual free trade zone.

Mongolia's parliament, the Great Hural, has approved revisions to tax laws that scrap virtually all import duties, slash taxes on business, offer incentives to foreign investors and raise the income tax threshold, officials said.
"Mongolia may be among the first countries that lifts import taxes," Finance Minister P. Tsagaan told a news conference.
The radical reforms take effect from May 1.

The revisions, passed last week by Mongolia's Democratic Union government, scrap all import duties except on five luxury or strategic items -- oil, oil products, wine, spirits and tobacco, officials said.
But the tariff on oil is cut to 31 percent from a previous 36.5 percent.
"We are a country of 2.3 million people, sandwiched between two giants," Prime Minister M. Enkhsaikhan told parliament on April 17, defending the government's decision.
"Although a natural reaction to this situation is to put up high protectionist barriers, we know that this would be condemning ourselves to isolation and backwardness forever," he said.
Joint ventures and foreign companies are exempt from import duty, Tsagaan said.
"After the implementation of this tax system, foreign investors may be interested in Mongolia," he said. "We hope Mongolia's production will increase."
The revisions slash income taxes on businesses, setting a 15 percent rate on income of up to 10 million tugriks ($12,500), from a previous 15 percent rate on income of up to just 1.5 million tugriks.
The tax rate will be 30 percent on income of 10 million-100 million tugriks and 40 percent above that level.
"The current rate exerts a negative influence on Mongolia's economy," D. Ganbold, chairman of the parliament Committee on Economic Policy, told reporters.
"People do not create big companies or set up new enterprises because of the high percentage of taxes," he said.
The previous rate on earnings of 1.5-3.0 million tugriks was 25 percent, 35 percent on income of 3.0-4.5 million and 40 percent above that.
The tax reforms include breaks for ordinary Mongolians.
People earning the average annual per capita income of 360,000 tugriks ($450), or less, will now be exempt from tax.
Incomes of 360,000-576,000 tugriks will be subject to a 10 percent tax rising to a maximum 40 percent for those with annual income of more than 1.152 million tugriks, officials said.
Previously all incomes of 144,000 tugriks and above were subject to a flat 10 percent income tax.
Income tax in Mongolia's sprawling rural areas will vary according to income and market prices of animals, while herders with less than 150 head of livestock will be exempt.
Tsagaan estimated the tax changes would cost the budget 20 billion tugriks a year, but said the government planned to offset the loss by economising.
For example, central heating would be switched on only from October 1 and not September 15 as before and turned off two weeks earlier -- on May 1.
"This will all have a good impact," Dangold said.
($1=800 tugriks)
